threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflows and main pain points across all service types.

messages.text:
Kicking off the workflow standardisation work for Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations.
I have uploaded the first pass of the current repair workflow maps based on interviews and notes from last month. They are captured in Current Repair Workflow Maps and linked to the mapping task.
For now, I have mapped:
- in-home appliance repairs
- workshop appliance repairs
- power tool bench repairs
- telecom and consumer electronics visits
Please take a look at Current Repair Workflow Maps and comment here on:
1) Steps that are missing or out of order for your area
2) Top pain points you see day to day (ideally 3–5 per area)
This will help us close out the mapping task and move into checklist design.
Tagging folks here to get your input.

Thanks for sharing Current Repair Workflow Maps.
Looking at the in-home appliance flow, I see most of the steps I follow, but a couple of things seem missing:
- I usually do a quick safety check on the power outlet and surrounding area before touching the appliance
- After the repair, I often spend time explaining usage and basic maintenance to the customer
Pain points from my side:
1) Parts availability: we often discover on-site that a specific board or seal is missing, so we have to rebook
2) Time windows are tight, especially when the previous job runs over
3) Paper forms are not aligned with what customer service promises on the phone, so I end up writing extra notes
Happy to clarify if anything is unclear.

I went through the power tool bench repair map in Current Repair Workflow Maps.
The main sequence looks right: intake, visual check, electrical tests, repair, final test, paperwork.
A few gaps from what I see at the bench:
- Intake: we often get tools without clear fault description, so we spend time calling the customer
- Testing: for battery tools, we also test the charger and sometimes the battery from another unit to isolate the issue
Top pain points for power tools:
1) Incomplete intake info and missing accessories (batteries, chargers, bits)
2) Rework when we do not document test results clearly and another tech picks up the same tool later
3) Storage and tagging: repaired tools sometimes sit on the shelf because the customer was not contacted or the label is unclear

I also checked the power tool workflow in Current Repair Workflow Maps.
One question: in the map, after electrical tests, it goes straight to repair. In practice, we sometimes need to do a test run under load before deciding which parts to order.
Should that be a separate step in the map, or do we treat it as part of diagnostics?
Pain points I notice:
- When we order parts, there is no clear place in the form to note expected delivery date
- Sometimes tools come back because the customer says the same issue reappeared, but we do not have a standard way to compare old and new readings
I might be missing something from the mapping session, so let me know if this is already covered somewhere else.

I reviewed the telecom and consumer electronics visit flow in Current Repair Workflow Maps.
The general order matches what I do: pre-call, travel, on-site diagnostics, repair or install, testing, wrap-up.
A few things I think are missing or too light:
- Pre-visit: I usually check signal levels or service status in the system before going out
- On-site: sometimes we need to move the router or set up repeaters, which adds time and extra steps
Pain points from my side:
1) Appointments booked without checking if the customer has access to the building or roof when needed
2) No standard way to log signal readings, so it is hard to compare visits
3) When there is no signal due to external issues, customers still expect a fix on the spot, and we do not have a clear script for that

From the mover side, I looked at the parts of Current Repair Workflow Maps where we move heavy appliances or tools between home and workshop.
The main steps are there, but a few details are not explicit:
- We often need to coordinate with technicians on-site to disconnect or secure equipment before lifting
- For fragile electronics, we sometimes improvise packing because there is no standard checklist
Pain points I see:
1) Last-minute changes to pick-up or delivery times, which cause extra trips or waiting
2) Not enough information about weight, dimensions, or special handling needs when the job is scheduled
3) Limited space in the van when multiple large items are booked on the same route

This is helpful, thanks.
From what I am hearing so far, some cross-cutting issues are emerging:
- Intake quality (missing info, missing accessories)
- Parts availability and tracking
- Time window and scheduling pressure
- Documentation gaps (test results, signal readings, labels)
Can each of you confirm your top three pain points, even if they overlap with others? I want to narrow this down so we can decide what to tackle first in the standard operating procedure.
Also, please flag if any of the mapped steps in Current Repair Workflow Maps are simply wrong for your area so we can correct the mapping task before we close it.

For in-home and workshop appliance repairs, my top three would be:
1) Parts not available when needed, leading to second visits
2) Time pressure from tight scheduling, especially when travel or complex diagnosis is involved
3) Paper forms not matching what customer service promises, so expectations are misaligned
On the maps, the only thing that feels off is that the safety check is shown after opening the appliance. In practice, I do a quick environment and power check before touching anything.

For power tools, my top three pain points are:
1) Poor intake information and missing accessories, which slows down diagnostics
2) Rework due to incomplete documentation of tests and repairs
3) Storage and tagging issues that delay returning tools to customers
The map looks mostly right to me. I agree with the comment about adding a clear test run step before deciding on parts, especially for tools that only fail under load.

Aligning with what was said for power tools, my three would be:
1) No clear place to record expected parts delivery dates
2) Lack of standard way to compare old and new readings when a tool comes back
3) Confusion when multiple technicians touch the same tool without a shared checklist
I am ok with you adding a separate test run step in the map. That matches what I do at the bench.

For telecom and electronics visits, my top three pain points are:
1) Appointments booked without checking building or roof access, which can block the job
2) No standard way to log signal readings and configurations
3) No clear script for cases where the issue is outside our control, like network outages
The map is mostly fine. I would just add a pre-visit system check step and a more explicit logging step after testing.

From the moving side, my three main pain points are:
1) Last-minute schedule changes that cause extra trips or idle time
2) Lack of information about weight, dimensions, and special handling needs when jobs are created
3) No standard packing and securing checklist for heavy or fragile items
The map could show more clearly when we need a technician on-site to disconnect or secure equipment before we move it.

Thanks all, this is very consistent.
To move us toward a shared view, I propose we cluster the pain points into themes:
A) Intake and documentation quality (missing info, missing accessories, missing readings, unclear labels)
B) Scheduling and coordination (time windows, last-minute changes, access constraints, mover and technician coordination)
C) Parts and materials flow (availability, tracking, expected delivery dates)
If we had to pick three to focus on in the first version of the standard operating procedure, my suggestion would be:
1) Intake and documentation quality
2) Scheduling and coordination
3) Parts and materials flow
Please react or comment if you disagree or would swap any of these.

Those three themes work for me.
If we improve intake and documentation, a lot of the rework on power tools should drop. Scheduling and parts flow are also big drivers of delays from what I see at the bench.

I agree with those three.
For appliances, intake and parts flow are the biggest sources of second visits. Scheduling and coordination also matter, but if we fix the first two, the day already becomes much smoother.

From the moving side, I am aligned as well.
Scheduling and coordination is key for us, but it depends a lot on good intake information, so grouping them like this makes sense.

Works for me too.
If we standardise how we log readings and pre-visit checks, that should help with both documentation and scheduling for telecom visits.

Great, sounds like we have convergence.
Let us lock in the top three focus areas for the first version of the standard operating procedure as:
1) Intake and documentation quality
2) Scheduling and coordination
3) Parts and materials flow
On scope for the initial pilot, my proposal is to include:
- In-home appliance repairs
- Workshop power tool repairs
- Telecom and consumer electronics visits
We can bring movers into the pilot where these jobs require transport, but not run a separate mover-only pilot.
Please confirm if you are ok with this pilot scope or if you see any major gaps.

Pilot scope sounds good to me.
Including workshop power tools and the related moves should give us enough volume without overcomplicating things.

I am ok with that scope.
In-home appliance repairs are where we see most of the customer impact, so it makes sense to include them early.

Fine by me.
Telecom and electronics visits fit well into this, and we can test the new logging and communication steps there.

I am comfortable with movers being part of the pilot where transport is needed, without a separate stream.
That should still give us enough data on handling and coordination.

Thanks all, I will update Current Repair Workflow Maps and the mapping task to reflect the corrections and the agreed focus areas and pilot scope.
Next step from here is to translate these into the first versions of the diagnostic checklists and visit procedures.

threads.thread_goal: Define and iterate on diagnostic checklists for appliances and power tools.

messages.text:
Following up on the workflow mapping, I have drafted first versions of the appliance and power tool diagnostic checklists.
They are captured as:
- Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist
- Power Tool Repair Checklist
Both are based on Current Repair Workflow Maps and the pain points we agreed to focus on.
Key questions:
1) For each checklist, what are the minimum steps that must always be done on every job?
2) What should be optional or only for specific fault types?
Please review and comment so we can finalise the first versions and move toward pilot-ready checklists.

I went through Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist.
For me, the steps that should always be done on every appliance job are:
- Basic safety and environment check (power outlet, water, gas where relevant)
- Intake confirmation with the customer (symptoms, history, any previous repairs)
- Visual inspection of the appliance and connections
- Basic functional test to reproduce the issue
- Final test after repair and short explanation to the customer
The more detailed component-level checks could be conditional based on the symptom.
One concern: the checklist has a lot of fields. I am worried it might slow us down if we have to tick every single one on paper.

On Power Tool Repair Checklist, I like that it separates intake, visual, electrical tests, and functional tests.
Minimum steps I would always do:
- Intake check: confirm tool type, accessories received, and fault description
- Visual inspection: housing, cord or battery contacts, obvious damage
- Basic electrical safety checks before powering on
- Functional test under no load and, where safe, under load
- Final test and documentation of readings or observations
More advanced tests, like detailed motor diagnostics, could be conditional.
We should also make sure there is a clear place to note which accessories were tested, to avoid confusion later.

I reviewed Power Tool Repair Checklist as well.
I have a question: for battery tools, should we always test both the battery and the charger, or only when the symptom suggests a power issue?
If we make it mandatory, it might add time, but if we skip it, we might miss some faults.
Also, I did not see a field for expected parts delivery date. Should that be part of this checklist or a separate form?

Good questions.
On battery tools, my initial thought is:
- Always test the battery and charger when the symptom is related to power or runtime
- Make it optional for purely mechanical issues, but still available on the checklist
For expected parts delivery date, I would lean toward adding a field in the checklist so that it is captured consistently, even if the actual ordering happens in another system.
Let us hear from others on whether that feels workable in practice.

On the battery and charger question, I would support making it conditional.
If the tool clearly has a mechanical issue, like a broken housing or switch, testing every battery and charger every time might not add much.
But we should make the conditional rule very clear in the checklist so people do not skip it when it is relevant.

Coming back to Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist, I think we should also include a simple field for parts used and estimated versus actual time.
That will help us later when we look at rework and time per job.
I am still a bit unsure how we will fit all of this on the existing paper forms without making them too crowded.

On the paper form constraint, we can prioritise which fields must be on the main form and which can be on the back or as a short code.
For appliances, I hear the following as minimum mandatory steps for every job:
- Safety and environment check
- Intake confirmation
- Visual inspection
- Basic functional test
- Final test and customer explanation
Can you confirm if you are comfortable treating these as the non-negotiable core, and making the rest conditional or optional?

Yes, I am comfortable with those as the core steps for every appliance job.
If we keep the rest as conditional, it should be manageable on paper.
We just need the checklist to be clear about which steps are always required and which depend on the symptom.

For Power Tool Repair Checklist, I would define the minimum required steps as:
- Confirm intake details and accessories
- Visual inspection
- Basic electrical safety checks
- Functional test (no load, and under load when safe)
- Final test and documentation of results
Battery and charger tests would be mandatory when the symptom suggests a power issue, and optional otherwise.
If we agree on that, I think we can move forward with this as the base for the pilot.

I am ok with that definition.
Having the functional test and documentation as mandatory should help reduce rework when tools come back.
For the parts delivery date, could we add a small field near the parts section so it is easy to find?

Sounds like we have a shared view.
To summarise for Power Tool Repair Checklist:
- Mandatory for every job: intake confirmation, visual inspection, basic electrical safety checks, functional test, final test and documentation
- Conditional: battery and charger tests when the symptom points to power issues, advanced diagnostics as needed
We will also add a field for expected parts delivery date in the parts section.
If there are no objections, I will treat this as the agreed minimum set of steps for the pilot version.

No objections from me.
Once we start the pilot, I can keep notes on any steps that feel redundant or any missing checks, so we can feed that into the refinement task later.

Great.
I will update Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist and Power Tool Repair Checklist with the agreed minimum steps and conditional rules, and we will use these versions for the pilot.
We will revisit them after we have some pilot data and feedback to refine and remove any redundant steps.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on telecom/electronics visit SOP and safety/handling procedures.

messages.text:
I have put together a draft of the telecom and consumer electronics service visit procedure based on our earlier mapping.
The document is Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP.
It covers:
- Pre-visit checks (system status, signal levels where available)
- On-site installation or repair steps
- Signal testing and logging
- Wrap-up and customer communication
Please review and let me know if any key steps are missing or out of order, especially around safety and logging.
In parallel, we also have a draft Handling and Transport Safety Checklist from the moving side to review.

On Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I focused on:
- Packing steps for fragile electronics and heavy appliances
- Lifting techniques and when to use extra equipment
- Securing items in the vehicle and coordination with technicians on-site
From my side, the sequence is:
1) Confirm item details and any special handling notes
2) Prepare packing materials
3) Coordinate with technician to disconnect or secure equipment
4) Lift and move using proper techniques
5) Secure items in the vehicle following the checklist
Happy to adjust if there are telecom-specific needs I have not covered.

Thanks for drafting these.
For Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, I want to make sure we are explicit about:
- Pre-visit checks to avoid wasted trips when there are known outages or access issues
- Standard fields for logging signal readings and configurations
- Clear handover when movers are involved in transporting equipment
Could you walk us through how the logging section works in Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, and where you see the interface with Handling and Transport Safety Checklist?

In Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, the logging section currently has:
- Fields for initial signal readings (downstream, upstream, noise margin)
- Configuration notes (router location, SSID, channel, any repeaters installed)
- Final readings after adjustments
The idea is that we log these on the existing paper form using short codes.
For the interface with Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I added a step in the on-site section: if equipment needs to be moved to another room or location, we call out that movers or a second person may be required for heavy items, and we reference the handling checklist.
I am not fully sure if the access checks before the visit are detailed enough, though.

From the moving side, the interface you describe makes sense.
If the SOP clearly states when a second person or mover is required, and links to Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, that should reduce unsafe lifting.
One suggestion: in the handling checklist, we can add a simple field to note whether the move is within the same room, same floor, or between floors, since that changes the risk.

On the access checks, I suggest we make the pre-visit section of Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP more explicit:
- Confirm building or roof access if needed
- Check for any known network outages in the area
- Confirm customer contact details and any special instructions
Would you be comfortable adding these as mandatory pre-visit steps for telecom and electronics jobs in the pilot?

Yes, I can add those as mandatory pre-visit steps.
They match what I try to do already, just not always in a structured way.
Making them explicit in Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP should help reduce wasted trips.

On Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I like the structure you outlined.
To align with our overall safety requirements, we should ensure it includes:
- Clear guidance on when to refuse a move due to unsafe conditions
- A reminder to use appropriate lifting aids for heavy items
- A simple check that items are secured before the vehicle moves
Do you see any gaps there from your experience, especially with heavy appliances and large TVs?

Those points are aligned with what we need.
I would add two small things:
- A note to check for obstacles on the path before moving (stairs, loose rugs, narrow doors)
- A reminder to communicate with the technician or customer before starting the move, so everyone knows what is happening
I can incorporate these into Handling and Transport Safety Checklist.

Great.
To make sure we are ready for the pilot, I propose we treat the current version of Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, with the added pre-visit checks and explicit logging fields, as the standard for telecom and electronics jobs in the pilot.
Unless there are strong objections, we will sign off this version for pilot use and adjust after we see the first results.

I am ok with using this version for the pilot.
Once we start using it in the field, I will keep track of any steps that feel unclear or missing so we can refine it later.

On Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, with the additions you mentioned (path check, communication, refusal criteria, lifting aids, securing items), I am comfortable treating this as the standard for the pilot as well.
We will use it whenever movers are involved in telecom, appliance, or power tool jobs in the pilot routes.
If there are no further comments, we will consider this checklist approved for pilot use.

Works for me.
I will update Handling and Transport Safety Checklist with the extra points and share the final version so everyone can see it before the pilot starts.

Thanks both.
We now have:
- Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP signed off for pilot use
- Handling and Transport Safety Checklist approved for moves during the pilot
I will integrate both into the consolidated field service SOP later on.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in scheduling rules and customer communication approach.

messages.text:
Based on the mapped workflows and the pain points we prioritised, I have drafted:
- Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules
- Customer Communication Playbook
Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules covers time slots, travel buffers, load limits, and coordination between movers and technicians.
Customer Communication Playbook includes templates for pre-visit, on-site, and post-visit communication, including how to handle delays and next steps.
We need to agree on the rules for the pilot routes and confirm the communication approach for all pilot jobs.
Please review and share any concerns or suggestions before we lock these in.

On Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules, I like the idea of adding travel buffers between in-home appliance jobs.
Right now, the schedule often assumes ideal traffic and no overruns.
One question: the draft mentions a standard 30-minute buffer between jobs. For some routes, that might be too much, and for others, not enough.
Is there a way to adjust the buffer based on distance or area without making the rules too complex?

From the mover side, Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules look reasonable.
The load limits per vehicle and per route are clear.
I would just highlight that when we combine heavy appliance moves with multiple smaller items, we need to be careful not to exceed the practical loading time, even if the weight is within limits.
Maybe we can add a simple rule about maximum number of large items per route.

Looking at Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules from the workshop side, I appreciate the attempt to smooth the flow of power tools coming in and out.
The rule about limiting the number of complex diagnostics per day per technician should help.
On Customer Communication Playbook, I like the idea of a standard message when tools are ready for pickup, including opening hours and any storage limits.
We should also include a simple way to inform customers when we are waiting for parts, so they do not keep calling for updates.

For telecom visits, the pre-visit communication template in Customer Communication Playbook looks good.
It mentions confirming access and contact details, which should help.
I am not sure if the on-site delay script fully covers cases where there is a network outage and we cannot fix the issue immediately.
Maybe we can add a short explanation and a commitment to follow up once the external issue is resolved.

On travel buffers, we can define a simple rule in Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules:
- Base buffer of 20 minutes between jobs
- Increase to 30 minutes for routes crossing certain zones or during peak hours
We can keep the list of zones short for the pilot to avoid complexity.
Would that address your concern without making scheduling too manual?

Yes, a base buffer plus a slightly larger one for specific zones sounds workable.
As long as the rules are clear for the schedulers, it should help reduce the rush between jobs.

Good point on the number of large items.
We can add a rule that limits each route to a maximum number of heavy or bulky items, even if the total weight is within limits.
For the pilot, we could set that maximum to a small number and adjust based on feedback.
I will add this to Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules.

On the network outage scenario, we can extend Customer Communication Playbook with a short script that explains:
- The issue is due to a wider network problem
- What the customer can expect in terms of resolution time
- How and when we will follow up
I will draft a short version and include it in the on-site and post-visit sections.

On the parts waiting communication, maybe we can standardise a message that says:
- Which part we are waiting for (in simple terms)
- Expected arrival window
- That we will contact them as soon as the tool is ready
If that is in Customer Communication Playbook, it should reduce ad-hoc calls.

Agreed.
I will add a standard template for parts waiting updates to Customer Communication Playbook, with fields for a simple part description and expected arrival window.
For the pilot, we will ask technicians or workshop staff to use this template whenever a job is delayed due to parts.

One more comment on Customer Communication Playbook for in-home appliances.
The pre-visit message mentions a two-hour arrival window. That is fine, but we should also include a note about possible delays and how we will inform the customer if we are running late.
That might reduce frustration when earlier jobs overrun.

Good point.
We can add a simple rule: if we expect to be more than a certain number of minutes late, we send a short update using the template in Customer Communication Playbook.
I will include that in the on-site section for technicians.

Given the feedback so far, I propose we:
- Use Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules as drafted, with the adjusted travel buffers and route limits for heavy items, for all pilot routes
- Use Customer Communication Playbook as the standard for pre-visit, on-site, and post-visit communication for all pilot jobs, including the new scripts for delays, parts waiting, and network outages
Unless there are strong objections, we will treat these as the agreed rules and communication approach for the pilot.

No objections from me.
The route limits and communication rules should help avoid last-minute surprises on moving days.

I am ok with using these rules and templates for telecom visits in the pilot.
The clearer scripts should make difficult conversations a bit easier.

Works for the workshop side as well.
Standard messages for parts and pickup should reduce back-and-forth with customers.

Thanks all.
I will finalise Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules and Customer Communication Playbook with the agreed adjustments and share the pilot versions.
We will monitor how they work during the pilot and adjust if needed.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot, review results, and confirm adjustments before rollout.

messages.text:
We have completed the initial pilot for Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations.
I have shared a draft Pilot Results and Recommendations Report summarising:
- Metrics on rework, time per job, and missed appointments
- Feedback from technicians, movers, and customers
- Proposed adjustments to Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist and Power Tool Repair Checklist
We now need to:
1) Confirm whether the top three pain points we chose were effectively addressed, or define what remains for the next iteration
2) Confirm the final version of Power Tool Repair Checklist for full rollout
Please review the report and share your observations.

From the appliance side, the pilot results in Pilot Results and Recommendations Report match what I experienced.
Intake and documentation improved a lot with Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist. I had fewer cases where I arrived with missing information.
Scheduling felt smoother with the buffers, though there were still a few tight days.
Parts and materials flow improved a bit, but we still had some delays when rare parts were needed.
Overall, I would say the first two pain points were mostly addressed, and the third one improved but still needs work.

Looking at the power tool section of Pilot Results and Recommendations Report, the reduction in rework is clear.
The mandatory steps in Power Tool Repair Checklist helped a lot with documentation and final testing.
Intake quality improved when customer service used the new questions, but we still had some tools arriving without accessories.
Scheduling and parts flow were better, but there is room to improve communication on parts delays.
I think the three pain points we picked were the right ones, and we made good progress on all of them.

From my side on power tools, the updated Power Tool Repair Checklist in the pilot felt clearer than the first version.
The conditional rules for battery and charger tests worked fine.
I still sometimes forgot to fill in the expected parts delivery date, but when I did, it helped with customer updates.
I did not see any major issues that would block using this checklist more widely.

For telecom visits, the pre-visit checks and logging steps from Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, combined with the new communication templates, reduced wasted trips and made conversations easier.
The report shows fewer missed appointments and better documentation of signal readings.
The main remaining gap I see is around rare network issues where we still do not have perfect scripts, but that is more of a fine-tuning point.

From the mover perspective, Handling and Transport Safety Checklist helped standardise how we pack and move heavy or fragile items.
The report shows fewer incidents and less damage.
Scheduling and coordination improved with the route limits and buffers, though we still had a couple of days where last-minute changes caused some stress.
Overall, the main pain points we discussed earlier are in a much better place now.

Thanks for the feedback.
Summarising what I am hearing and what Pilot Results and Recommendations Report shows:
- Intake and documentation quality: clear improvement across appliances, power tools, and telecom
- Scheduling and coordination: improved, with fewer missed appointments, but still some edge cases with last-minute changes
- Parts and materials flow: better tracking and communication, but rare parts remain a challenge
Given this, I would say we have addressed the three main pain points for the majority of cases, with some remaining work on rare parts and exceptional scheduling situations.
Does anyone disagree with that summary or feel that one of the three areas is still not sufficiently covered for rollout?

I agree with that summary.
For appliances, the remaining issues are mostly special cases, like rare parts or very remote locations.
Those might be better handled as exceptions rather than changing the core process again.

Same from my side.
The main pain points are much better now.
For the remaining gaps, we can probably handle them with a short exception section in the SOP rather than more checklist changes.

Ok, then I propose we:
- Consider the three original pain points as largely addressed for standard cases
- Capture rare parts and exceptional scheduling situations in an exception handling section of the SOP for the next iteration
On Power Tool Repair Checklist, the report suggests a couple of small tweaks: clarifying the wording on battery tests and moving the expected parts delivery date field closer to the main parts section.
If we make those minor edits, are you comfortable treating this version as final for full rollout?

Yes, with those small edits, I am comfortable using Power Tool Repair Checklist as the standard going forward.
The structure works well, and the pilot did not surface any major issues.

I am ok with that too.
Moving the parts delivery date field should make it easier to remember to fill it in.
The rest of the checklist feels stable enough for rollout.

Great.
To close this out:
- We will treat the three original pain points as addressed for standard cases, and document remaining edge cases in an exception section for the next SOP update
- We will adopt the updated Power Tool Repair Checklist, with the minor wording and layout tweaks, as the final version for full rollout
I will reflect this in Pilot Results and Recommendations Report and in the rollout plan.

Sounds good.
For appliances, I am ready to use the current checklist and communication templates more broadly once the training sessions are scheduled.

I am ready for the wider rollout on the telecom side as well.
The pilot gave us enough confidence in the new visit procedure and communication approach.
From the mover side, I am comfortable continuing with the handling checklist and the new scheduling rules in the wider rollout.

Thanks everyone.
Next steps are to finalise the pilot report, update the SOP and checklists with the agreed changes, and plan the full rollout and training sessions.
I will share a draft rollout schedule and training agenda shortly.
